speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When the committee
rose we were discussing the following:
Customs tariff-549. Wool, the hair of the camel, alpaca, goat or other like animal, not further prepared than combed: British preferential tariff, free; intermediate tariff, free; general tariff, free.

Last night the committee had this matter under consideration. As a matter of fact the discussion in connection with the woollen industry, as in the case of the previous schedule dealing with cottons, was of a rather general character. This is made necessary by the fact that amendments to one item necessarily affect other items. The minister, however, during the closing moments of yesterday's sitting gave utterance to certain views which I think merit attention and, indeed, demand some consideration from us. I wish to deal with some of the things which the minister said last night, and to invite his attention once more to the damage to the woollen industry of Canada which undoubtedly will result in consequence of his action under this budget.
Now, one of the points emphasized by the minister last night was that our woollen industry was not necessarily suffering very much, and indeed if it was suffering, he attempted to offset the seriousness of its condition by suggesting that the woollen industry in the United States was also suffering; therefore we should not complain. I must say that I have no sympathy whatever
with that sort of argument. It is pretty hard, Mr. Chairman, to discuss this subject if the whole house is going to carry on conversations.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

The point at issue between the Minister of Finance and ourselves is whether or not the measures immediately before the committee are going adversely to affect Canadian industry, particularly at this moment the woollen industry. I noticed that in one of his observations when answering an interjection by my hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) the minister said:
I am glad to have that statement from my hon. friend.
That is, that we were not asking that the woollen schedule should be raised, as high as the United States tariff.
It has been argued here that we would improve the condition of the woollen industry in Canada by putting a duty on wool.
This is one of the minister's characteristic statements. When he finds himself confronted with an argument that is not answerable, he seeks to evade the issue by suggesting that we are asking for something that is unreasonable and neither in the interests of the people of Canada nor of the country's industrial development. Our point is this, Mr. Chairman, and we are not going to allow the minister to becloud the issue in the public mind. We submit that the woollen industry is a basic industry, that it must be recognized as an industry indigenous to Canada, and must receive such consideration as will place it upon a healthy and prosperous basis.	*J,
I should like to draw the attention of the committee to this distinction between the woollen industry and the cotton industry. Let it be understood that I am not attacking the cotton industry in making this distinction. The cotton industry must necessarily depend entirely upon imported raw materials; we grow no cotton. But Canada by reason of its climate and the physical nature of the country is peculiarly suited to the development of the woollen industry. With the exception perhaps of some of the finer wools furnished by Spain and Australia, we can produce wool of excellent quality suitable for almost every branch-I want that to be noted-suitable for almost every branch of the woollen trade. But what is of far more importance, Canada must continue to be a heavy consumer of wool. It does not matter what artificial silks or other new products may be introduced, they will com-
1632	COMMONS
Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
pete far more with cotton than with wool; but by reason of our climatic conditions we must be a wool-using people, and the larger our population grows and the more our country develops, the greater will be the demand for woollen goods. Furthermore-it is so obvious that it scarcely needs to be mentioned-during the past years furs have played a very large part in the winter clothing of our people in the colder sections of the Dominion; but furs are getting more expensive and scarcer year by year, and consequently we are depending more upon woollens than ever before to protect us during the winter season. I emphasize that. There is no parallel between the ootton and woollen industries; the latter is an industry indigenous to this country.
My second point is that the cotton industry is very largely controlled by a few large concerns. This is peculiar to the industry and quite proper; I have no fault to find with it. But the woollen industry in Canada has been established for over a hundred years, it is scattered throughout the Dominion, and is based on the principle of individual factories rather than large concerns as in the cotton industry. In other words, it is an individual rather than a trust or combination business. It might be wise, Mr. Chairman, to bring about an amalgamation of some of our woollen concerns and place them on a larger producing basis, but that is an economic question that does not enter into a consideration of this tariff. The point is that during the last century we have established a large number of individual woollen factories, built up by Canadian enterprise, and these individual industries are being jeopardized bj the tariff revision immediately before us.
I think I might summarize very briefly the attitude of the minister or of the government towards the cotton industry and the woollen industry. In respect of the cotton industry it is a policy of deceit; in respect of the 'woollen industry, a policy of destruction. ^Referring again to the artificial silk industry, 'this does not enter into competition with the woollen industry to anything like the degree that it does with the cotton industry; and where artificial silk does affect woollen goods it is only those finer and higher classes upon which a duty might very properly be imposed, and which might be classified almost as luxuries. But the ordinary woollen goods worn by the ordinary citizen year in and year out are of a character not brought into competition with artificial silk at all.
My hon. friend the minister made reference to the United States. He quoted the duties imposed in the United States, which
[Mr. Stevens. 1
are very high, and in order to impress them on the minds of the committee I might indicate what they are; they are well worth considering. The duties imposed in the United States are exceptionally high as compared with our own. They are as follows:
Woven fabrics, weighing more than four ounces per square yard, wholly or in chief value of wool, valued at not more than 60 cents per pound, 24 cents per pound and 40 per centum ad valorem; valued at more than 60 cents but not more than 80 cents per pound, 37 cents per pound and 50 per centum ad valorem; valued at more than 80 cents but not more than $1.50 per pound, 45 cents per pound upon the wool content thereof and 50 per centum ad valorem; valued at more than $1.50 per pound, 45 cents per pound upon the wool content thereof, and 50 per centum ad valorem.
I wonder if the committee realizes the extent of these duties imposed by the United States. Then take blankets and similar articles. The duties are as follows:
Blankets and similar articles, including carriage and automobile robes and steamer rugs, made of blanketing, wholly or in chief value of wool, not exceeding three yards in length, valued at not more than 50 cents per pound, 18 cents per pound and 30 per centum ad valorem; valued at more than 50 cents but not more than $1 per pound, 27 cents per pound, and 32i per centum ad valorem; valued at more than $1 but not more than $1.50 per pound, 30 cents per pound and 35 per centum ad valorem; valued at more than $1.50 per pound. 37 cents per pound and 40 per centum ad valorem.
That is the duty on woollen blankets, that is, blankets made of wool, or partly of wool. It will be observed that the duty in the United States is altogether beyond anything that we have ever suggested should be imposed in Canada. I have not checked the figures, but I venture the statement that they are perhaps two, three or four times as much as the corresponding items in our tariff. The minister said last night: I suppose my hon. friends opposite want us to put on a tariff as high as that of the United States. We have made no such suggestion, Mr. Chairman. What we are asking for, as I have already indicated, is an adjustment of the tariff that will permit the Canadian industry to be maintained in a condition of real prosperity in Canada.
To enable them to live.

Yes, it has indeed come
to that, that some of them are asking merely for the privilege of continuing their existence in Canada. I continue this brief examination of the United States condition, and in checking up the United States government returns, at pages 624 and 625, I find that they had a production of raw wool, in 1926, of 269,000,000

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
pounds, and imports of 299,000,000 pounds; that is, they imported approximately the same amount as they produced. But their imports of manufactured wool were 37,000 long tons, or about 82,000,000 pounds valued at $70,000,000. I ask the committee to consider this point for a moment. The United States imported woollen manufactured goods at the rate of 60 cents per capita-$70,000,000 worth as against 120,000,000 people, while in Canada, which is more a wool using country, we imported $40,000,000 of manufactured woollen goods, or at the rate of $3.50 per capita, or about six times as much per capita as the United States. It may be said that there is no argument in that, but the point I want to make is this: The minister suggested that the woollen industry in the United States was not flourishing because it had a high tariff. That was his implication, but I do not think it is his opinion. It was just that kind of general statement used frequently by those who argue for free trade to prejudice the public mind against the principle of protection. That is all it was, and that is all it was intended to do. But the facts belie hi3 statement.
The United States, as I have already indicated, use in the production of woollen goods some 568,000,000 pounds of wool; that is their total consumption of wool used in manufacturing. They export only 14,000,000 pounds out of 56S,000,000 pounds that they use in manufacturing; so practically all the wool they import and almost all the wool they grow they use in their own factories. Their importations are only 82,000,000 pounds, or about 12 per cent of the total amount of their production. So it will readily be seen, Mr. Chairman, that the United States is virtually self-contained so far as the woollen industry is concerned. They have built up a strong, virile industry there which is being maintained, and which is serving the needs of the people.
Now I wish to turn to another point in the minister's speech. He referred in a very casual way to the question of wages as if that were a subject of no importance. I am not going to go over the arguments that have already been presented as to what a very small factor, after all, is the duty so far as the internal production of woollen goods is concerned. For instance, I think my hon. friend from South Wellington demonstrated that most excellently last night when he showed that the amount of the duty on a suit of clothes costing from fifty to sixty dollars was between fifty and sixty cents. That would be the effect of the duty, so iit does not influence the consumer, but what
is its effect upon the worker? My hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre yesterday made a statement which impressed me very much. He said that if the workers of Canada could be persuaded that they were receiving any benefit from the imposition of a duty upon the manufactured article, they would support the imposition of such a duty, or words to that effect. The minister gave us some figures last night which were very interesting, and which I think ought to be considered very carefully by this house. Comparing wages, and taking Great Britain at the figure of 100, he said that the wages in France would represent 50, Italy 40, and Canada 160, as compared with 100 in Great Britain.
What is the hon. gentleman's interpretation of those figures?

I am using the minister's figures, although last year I gave an exact comparison of the actual wages paid in Great Britain, France, Germany and Canada. But I am using the minister's own figures, and an interpretation of those figures I think would show this, that in Canada we have to pay four times as much in wages per diem as they do in Italy, over three times as much as they do in France, and over 160 per cent of the wages paid in England. Now I ask my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre to give this thought consideraton. Before the manufacturer gets one atom of protection, you must give him a protection that will bridge the difference between those wages, that is, in so far as the wage content of cloth is concerned. Now the wage content of manufactured cloth, I am informed, is 55 per cent of the value of the cloth.
Is it not true that figures were presented to the tariff board showing that protection was granted equivalent to the entire wage bill?

W'e are unfortunately at a disadvantage in not having the evidence indexed and before us in proper form, but I recall the time when the presentation was made. I believe it was made by Mr. Deachmian.
. Mr. ADSHEAD : I have the figures here.

I have on two separate occasions carefully analyzed these wage figures based upon the data and statistics supplied me by the Labour department of Canada. Speaking from memory I may say that the result of my deductions indicated that the difference was almost double so far as Great Britain is concerned, about three times so far as France and Italy are concerned, and with a similar difference as regards Germany.

By reason, of the
lower cost of living in those countries, is not the nominal wage really higher than it seems?

That does not enter into this point. I know what my hon. friend has in mind and in some respects his argument is sound, but it does not apply here. The figures I compared were the actual wages paid in Great Britain, Germany, France and Italy and the actual wages paid in Canada for the same work. I gave the figures last year and they are all on Hansard. And they were taken from the Labour department's own statistics. I am now taking the statement presented yesterday by the Minister of Finance, and now I submit to the minister that it is his obvious duty, if he is to do the right thing by Canadian workmen, to impose a tariff under the woollen schedules, equal to the difference between the wage scale in Canada and the wage scale in Great Britain, France, Italy and Germany, before he gives the manufacturer any protection at all. The position is inescapable. Let us for the moment leave aside What that difference is. I do insist, however, that it is the minister's duty, if he is to protect Canadian workmen- leaving the manufacturer out of it altogether for the time being-to impose a duty equal to the difference between the wage scale in Canada and those in other countries.

Does my hon. friend not
think that he ought to take into consideration all the various factors that enter into The cost of production in Great Britain and wfc :ch are higher than in Canada? Take the item of taxation, for instance, and various forms of insurance which have not to be paid over here.
I am not objecting to that. Let me point out, however, that the cost of building in Canada as well as the cost of heating is very much higher than it is in England.
What about the income tax?

Well, the income tax is fairly oneTous here too, although it is not so severe as it is in England. But I am not disputing the point; I simply suggest that we stick to the question under discussion for the moment. So far as wages are concerned, we have a right to do justice to our Canadian workmen and to impose a protection on the manufactured articles equal to the difference between Canadian wages and wages paid in other countries.

Wages constitute
only one of the factors in the' cost of produc-
tion, and if other costs in Great Britain are higher than they are here surely the hon. gentleman cannot ignore them in his computation.

I am not disregarding
them, and my hon. friend's position is sound, But I do not admit that the costs in other directions are generally higher in Great Britain than they are here. My own impression is that the costs there are lower, although their income tax exceeds ours. The minister will correct me if I am wrong, but I question whether their corporation income tax is higher than ours.
What about local taxation in Great Britain?

Local rates in Great
Britain are not, in my opinion, a bit higher than ordinary municipal rates in Canada. As a matter of fact, you can follow the general ratio of costs in Great Britain as compared with Canada and you will find that capital in Great Britain is cheaper than it is in this country. No one will dispute that. And that is a big factor. Then take taxes and insurance. There is no appreciable difference between the two countries; if anything, the insurance rates would be higher in Canada because of the general use of wooden buildings as compared with stone and brick construction in the old country. In Canada, again, we have a dual taxation imposed in many of the provinces both by the provinces and by the federal authorities, and it is higher than the corporation income tax in Great Britain. Personal income tax is a different matter; it does not enter into consideration until you have earned profit and paid it to the individual. So that personal income tax is not a factor; it must be eliminated.

The hon.
member, I take it, would apply that principle fairly to all industry?

I have no objection to
the application of it generally.

Then the
next question is, would he apply it to the farming industry and allow the farmers the total cost of labour in the form of a bonus?

I am prepared to discuss
that question on its merits and in its proper place. I have certain views which I might be induced to express on the subject some day. The committee, however, has before it a practical issue. We are not discussing any general theory of economics; what we are considering is whether we shall do so and so

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
with a given industry. I was discussing the question of building costs. The cost of heating factories in Canada, the cost of building a structure capable of being heated, is certainly much higher than it is in Great Britain. Parenthetically I may observe this: One reason why industry is developing on the Pacific coast of Canada and the United States -and there is a new development there-is the fact that climatic conditions are such that the overhead in relation to heating and the cost of structures is less than it is in the central portions of Canada and the United States where the climate is cold. So that on a fair analysis of cost figures it will be found that the British, French and Italian woollen mills have a distinct advantage over Canada. Xow I return to the question of wages.

Does the hon
gentleman consider the question of overcapitalization that prevails in this country watered stock, and so forth?

My hon. friend is introducing a question which is certainly a fair subject of debate. But in fixing the rates of duty the tariff board could very well ignore any question of over-capitalization; indeed, they would have to do so if they did their duty. I am not here advocating the practice of watering stock, but I may say that companies that have been established, as many of our Canadian woollen industries have been established, for a hundred years, and which have constantly turned back their profits into the business, are entitled to stock issue for these returns to the business. As an hon. member reminds me, we are now dealing with the question of costs of production and not with that of watered stock. I agree with my hon. friend that if there is undue inflation of capital, that fact ought to be ignored in the fixation of the duty. Let me, however, finish my rather disjointed argument on the question of wages. The minister cited it himself and I say to him and to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that before the manufacturer receives one atom of protection, you must impose a dut3' equal to the difference between wages here and wages in other countries that are competing with us.

What percentage of woollen
goods consumed in Canada is imported from Italy?

I have the figures with
me but I do not think my hon. friend desires me to check them up.

I think it is very important.
The hon. member has endeavoured to impress upon the house the necessity for a
balancing as between duties imposed and wages paid between the two different countries. If he is going to give Italy as an example he should give to the house the benefit of the imports.

If this is any comfort to
my hon. friend, I am willing to eliminate all other countries than,Great Britain which is the country from which we import the major portion of our woollen goods. We can thus eliminate Italy, France and Germany. All these countries do supply us with some woollen goods, the exact amount of which I have not in mind, but the preponderance of imports comes from Great Britain, and we can stick to Great Britain for all the practical purposes of this issue. I want to carry this wage question one step further. According to a well-established principle in the manufacture of woollen goods, fifty-five per cent is claimed to be represented in wages. That, I think, is a fair proportion. In that case, if we take the difference between wages in Canada and wages in Great Britain, it would be a simple matter to determine what amount of duty should be imposed in order first of all to protect the Canadian workman without giving any protection whatever to the manufacturers. That rate would be something in the neighbourhood of 22 per cent or 23 per cent.
I turn to one of these items. The minister under item 551b eliminates a duty of 12| per cent on yarns and warps and he puts them on the free list. The committee ought clearh' to understand what we are doing in this regard. We are giving a distinct advantage to one factory, a factory which is in the riding of the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Kaiser); but it is rather significant- and I make this merely as a statement of fact without conveying any impression other than the fact itself conveys-that this factory is located in the riding contested by the chairman of the tariff advisory board, a riding which he purposes contesting again. The house ought to know this fact and they can put on it whatever construction they like. The point is this, that one factory is benefited and since this revision has been made, I am informed that they have already cancelled their orders for these yarns to other factories from whom they have been buying these yams during recent years. These are worsted yarns which are used in the manufacture of plush. I presume the plush is used in upholstering automobiles and so on, these yams being used as the foundation upon which these plush goods are built up. The question which this house must decide is whether it is doing its duty by the

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. My hon. friend has exhausted his forty minutes.

Very well. I will speak
again in a few minutes, probably for another

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
forty minutes, although I would have been through in about five minutes more.

I was extremely interested in the figures presented by my hon. friend; one of the things which struck me was his statement that with regard to woollens the wage costs -were 55 per cent of the cost of production. I have here a statement made by the gentleman who represented the woollen industry before the tariff advisory board, and I may say this is one of the benefits my hon. friends might derive from the members of the Consumers' League which they derided so much the other day. Mr. Barrett stated that the total wage cost amounts to 25 per cent of the selling value of the finished article.
Was that for knitted or woven goods?

I could not say; it is
for woollen goods. My hon. friend gave the cost as 55 per cent, and even if there were a difference between the two classes of goods surely it would not be so great as that.
There is that difference.
This gentleman represented the woollen industry before the tariff advisory board, and in his testimony stated that the figure of 25 per cent represented the wages plus the salaries of his company.

My hon. friend has just
stated that that 25 per cent refers to the selling cost, which is very different from 25 per cent of the production cost.

But then my hon. friends ask for a tariff which would provide for the difference between the wage cost of England and the wage cost of Canada, and surely a tariff of 35 per cent represents more than that difference.

That is the
production cost in the mill, but by no means the selling cost.

In England the cost of
labour represents only 15 per cent, so this tariff means that the protection afforded the industry in Canada is double the wage cost of production in England. Then, with regard to the imports of woollens, my hon. friend has stated that these amounted to $40,000,000 in 1927.
No, in 1926.

That is quite correct,
but you must take that in proportion to the total volume of trade. In 1878 we find that
the imports of wollens amounted to 10 per cent of the general trade of Canada. That figure dropped in 1897 to 8 per cent and in 1927 to 5 per cent, so in 1927 our imports of woollens in relation to the total trade of Canada were less by a half than in 1878, when we introduced the national policy of protection.
Then reference was made to the difficulties in which the manufacturers find themselves. They were asked by the tariff advisory board to produce their books to show how much they were losing, but with one exception they absolutely refused to do so.
No, my hon friend is wrong there.

I have the statement
here.

Although 1
will not do so, I could name at least two mills in which they put in their own men to investigate the books.

The statement was also
made before the tariff advisory board that the trouble with the woollen industry is that in many cases plants were built during the war when costs were high and production was heavy; in many cases these mills were equipped for the operation of two shifts. Now they have found themselves unable to operate and make the profits they made during the war, and they ask that the rest of Canada be especially taxed to assist them.

I am delighted that the
new rules permit one to take a little rest in the middle of a speech. My hon. friend, as to whose honesty of purpose there can be no question, has been a little misled by the terminology of the report which he has been reading. It is obvious that when you are considering the relation of the wages paid to the cost of production you cannot do so by taking the retail selling price or the wholesale selling price of the goods. I quoted official figures which were supplied by the Department of Labour, and these I offered not on my own authority but on the authority of the statisticians of the government. I think my hon. friend was quoting from a special pleading-
I was quoting the evidence of Mr. Barrett, who represented the woollen manufacturers before the tariff advisory board.

The point my hon. friend made was based upon the selling price of the goods. I think he will agree after reflection that such a comparison is neither fair nor

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
proper, so there is no use pursuing that argument further. Then, with regard to the last statement of my hon. friend that the companies would not allow investigation of their books, there is a statement contained in this report which I have not immediately under my hand, in which they declared that they were given every possible assistance by those who appeared before them, and were allowed to examine books and so on. They not only made no complaint but they refer especially to it, in the following words:
In conclusion, may we express appreciation of the effective co-operation received from those who have appeared before the board.
I think my hon. friend, in justice to those who appeared, will not be inclined to press the suggestion that they withheld information, which I think would be unfair.

The report said they
would not make their books available.

The report does not say
that, and I am sure we desire to be fair in this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will permit
me, I think it is fair to the mills to say that I have had no report from the tariff board that the mills were unwilling to give any information asked for. Indeed, I think the fact is quite to the contrary.

I believe it is so stated
somewhere in this report. I cannot place my finger on it for the moment but I believe I quoted it the other day.
I should like to return to what I was discussing a moment ago and that is the observations of the minister last night, or the purpose that he may have had in quoting certain statements from the press. Now I shall proceed first to refer to his quotations from the statements of gentlemen who appeared before the board. The minister said:
Then I have some comments upon the conduct of the woollen inquiry by some of those who appeared before the board. Mr. J. A. Burns, former president of the Canadian Woollen & Knit Goods Association, Toronto, said:
[DOT]'On behalf of the woollen manufacturers I would like to express our deep appreciation of the fair manner in which this investigation has been conducted."
Next the minister quoted a statement by Mr. Shaw who had this to say:
Might I associate myself and my confreres with the expression of appreciation just given by Mr. Burns?
Then the minister quoted Mr. Hodgson as follows:

May I be permitted to thank you and the board on behalf of Mr. Wood and myself for the very kind way in which you have received us?
These are simply expressions of courtesy. Surely the minister does not wish us to conclude that because these gentlemen courteously thanked the board for a fair hearing, therefore this schedule-based upon the minister's own common sense without one shred of evidence, without one shred of a finding or a fact from the advisory board- is wholly approved by them? The minister read this into Hansard for the purpose of giving out to the public the impression that the woollen industry, and these gentlemen in particular, were entirely satisfied with the schedule of duties before us.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not at all. They were entirely satisfied with the hearing, and that is all I said.

That is what I have been trying to point out to the minister, not only to-day but the other day as well. The results of this hearing are somewhere, heaven knows where, perhaps in the mind of Mr. Moore-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are before the committee.

There is not one fact or result before the committee, not a single finding not a single comment-not one. That is what we are complaining of. To my mind this house ought to go on record as censuring the board for dereliction of duty in presenting this report. Here is what the board say and the report speaks for itself:
Moreover, the transcripts contain the arguments of the applicants and their opponents, which, in our opinion, cannot be satisfactorily summarized, and after mature deliberation we have concluded that to attempt a summary would be not only unfair to those who have argued before the board, but as well would render to you and to parliament an incomplete service. The obvious intent of argument-*

I have' been unable to find any explanatory comments. They may be scattered through a mass of evidence unassimilated, undigested and unindexed, without comment, not brought into juxtaposition one with the other, but scattered-part of a hearing to-day and the balance of the hearing two weeks hence-and

I conclude with the observation, that as far as the woollen schedules of the present tariff are concerned, they bear every evidence of ruin for a number of factories, if not for the whole industry. Here is a factory which, we will say, has one half of its capital wrapped up in the spinning of yarn and the other half devoted to the purchase of machines for the utilization of these yarns. The effect of this clause to which I have referred will be to put out of business that part of the factory which is spinning yarns and allow the other half to continue operating. Does anyone presume to suggest that this, for a time at least, will not spell ruin to that industry? It means that the industry must convert its capital, its investment and its machinerj' into some other use and sustain the loss of such conversion, whatever it may be. I therefore impress upon the minister the seriousness of his action, and even yet hope that he may see his way clear to remedy this injustice which is being done to this industry. After all, the matter is one involving the welfare not of one or two concerns but of the whole industry of the Dominion.

The only excuse I have for

As a matter of fact we

I will come down to facts if the hon. gentleman wants them. A year ago last October I was in the city of Vancouver, right in the constituency of my hon. friend and I happened to meet some manufacturers of woollen goods who came to me

and said that they wanted more protection for their industry. I asked them where their main competition came from and against whom they would like to be protected. The answer was: Eastern Canada. I should like to know how you can protect those manufacturers of knitted and woollen goods in British Columbia against what they term cheap importations from the eastern part of the Dominion. They complain about the low wages paid in the east. I have heard manufacturers in the city of Winnipeg complaining about competition from Montreal on account of the low wages paid to the women engaged in industry in that particular city. Protection has given no benefit to those large manufacturing centres in eastern Canada, because if protection did protect the worker, why is it necessary to have in those provinces minimum wage acts? The hon. member also enunciated the theory that because wages are lower in Great Britain than they are in Canada, we should have some protection given to the manufacturer here against the lower wages of Great Britain and, I believe, Italy as well. What is the hon. member going to ask us to do when the competition comes from a country where wages are higher than in Canada? What about importations from the United States? I have been in this house for just three sessions, but during that time I have heard members of the Conservative party say: Look at the United States; look at the high wages they are paying there. If the United States are paying higher wages than Canada, then according to all logical reasoning we ought to cut off the tariff entirely against goods coming from the United States. I do not however suppose the hon. gentlemen will for a moment suggest doing anything of that kind because the main competition is not so much on goods from Great Britain as from the United States.
Not on the woollen tariff schedule.

What does the hon.
member mean by that?

That is that we should buy
nothing from another country but sell everything to it. That cannot be done. I believe the greatest punishment a nation can impose unon another is to establish a blockade against it. In the past few years we have had examples of this. When a nation has been unfriendly to another nation it has endeavoured to compel that nation to become economically independent by blockading its ports. That is punishment one nation has inflicted on another for doing something of an unfriendly character. I do not think the Conservative party are doing themselves credit, or doing any good to the cause of closer imperial relations by taking the attitude they have on this particular question. I should like to see Canadian goods consumed in Canada as much as possible. 1 want to give protection to the workers in this country. Where there are lower standards of living in other countries than there are in Canada, the manufacturers are entitled to protection against imposing a lower standard of wages on the workers. The statement of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is one to which I entirely subscribe. It is unfortunately true that the protection that has been given in the
Dominion of Canada has not in the least degree given any protection to the worker; the protection has been entirely a benefit to the manufacturer. When the workers get a certain amount of protection, you will find that they will take the attitude that the workmen do in Australia, where they are for protection, but the first protection given in Australia is not for the manufacturer, but for the work people engaged in industry. I have made these few observations on account of these two new ideas enunciated by the Conservative party last night and to-day. This idea of economic independence to me is one which it is impossible to carry out, and if it were attempted to be carried out, it would mean economic stagnation in the Dominion of Canada.

I wish to say a few words
on this matter, and my remarks will very largely take the form of questions addressed to the hon. member for Vancouver Centre.
I do not admit the right of any government to place a tariff on any goods whatsoever to be consumed at home, but if there is an industry essential to the welfare of this country which is seeking protection, then I think that that industry should be willing to lay its books on the table and let us see its profits, and whether or not it is over-capitalized. If it seeks protection, we should know the reason why.
But suppose, as the hon. member for Vancouver Centre states, that the actual wages paid here are much higher than the wages paid in European countries. That is a handicap to the manufacturer, I admit, but who does the hon. gentleman suggest should shoulder that difference? What industry is there in Canada to-day that is so prosperous that it can shoulder the difference? The hon. gentleman has overlooked the facts as they are. Perhaps he will answer that question yet. He says that it is the duty of the government to grant as much protection as will cover that difference. Upon whom will the burden fall? I have said before in this house, and I repeat it now, that those who advocate protection in Canada will never know what protection means until the farmer is placed in such a position that he can charge a price for his product sold in the home market that will give him a profit over the whole of his production whether sold at home or abroad, and when he is in a position to do that, he will be doing exactly the thing which the protected manufacturer is now doing. In what way does my hon. friend think the primary producer can overcome that same difficulty regarding wages? How does he think that we who have to com-

I do not know why they are out of business, but I would think it was because of incompetency in their methods and lack of up-to-date machinery.

They ought to engage
the hon. gentleman as general manager.

Whenever the farmer complains, we are told in this house that he is behind the times and that he should adopt modern methods. I say the same with respect to other industries. Most of the finished articles in the woollen schedules carry a duty of 35 per cent. That is an import penalty, and yet the protectionist advocates would blindly increase the burden on the class to which they are looking for the home market. Is it reasonable? But I have never yet heard from any hon. gentleman in this house a logical argument for protection. Protection kills itself in the end; it works against industry, no matter how high the tariff. Strange to say, to-day the British manufacturer can get over the tariff wall of any country just as easy as he can get into a free trade country. But where the argument of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) falls flat is in the fact that he has begged for protection against countries pay-

ing a lower wage than obtains in Canada. Yet he himself has been an advocate in this house for protection against the United States because of the higher wages there. How can he reconcile those two statements? How inconsistent the argument for protection has always been.
If the woollen industry of the Dominion is suffering from a lack of protection, I ask again, how is it that our woollen manufacturers can compete in countries, against which hon. gentlemen say they must be protected. Our woollen manufacturers have done very well in the export market in years gone by. Either they can compete without any protection, or else they are fleecing the home consumer by charging him a price to give them a profit on the whole output, whether sold at home or abroad. As I said last night to the minister, I take it as being only fair and reasonable, that these woollen schedules should be withdrawn for a time and be reconsidered. It is unreasonable to allow the revenue of the country to be impaired by complete free trade in raw materials when the home consumer is charged over one-third as a penalty on what he has to buy. It is unfair, it is class legislation in the worst form, and brands the government as serving only one group, comprising the capitalists and manufacturers of this country. I still wish him to explain, if he can, why this is being done at the present time. Not only in the tariff, but in the income tax also the capitalist is being relieved and a proportionately greater burden is being shifted to the working classes. Is there any British fair play in such a policy? it is unreasonable. This means placing the burden on those who are working double the hours that obtain in urban industries. Even our women and children on the farms are being discriminated against. I can take hon. gentlemen into districts where our children do not even know how to play. You are placing this burden on the sweated labour of the families now homesteading on the farms of Canada. I say again, it is unfair.

Mr. Chairman, my attention has been drawn to an error on my part. I said that the companies had refused to have their books investigated. What I intended to say was that they had refused to make their statements public, with the exception of one company. The Penman Manufacturing Company made their statement public.

It is difficult, Mr. Chairman, as anyone will at once admit who has given any study to economics, to frame a tariff schedule "'Inch will be fair 56103-105
all around, for so many things dovetail into other things that when you attempt to frame a tariff in regard to one article, you find yourself confronted with the fact that by so doing you are adversely affecting some other article closely related to it.
In regard to the woollen industry, it has always appeared to me that one of the first questions we should ask ourselves is, whether or not in a country like Canada it is advisable to encourage the sheep industry for the production of wool to be used in turn for the manufacture of woollens in the Dominion. In asking myself that question I have never been able to come to any other than one conclusion: that Canada is specially adapted, climatically and otherwise, for the raising of sheep. Therefore, it is a country where the sheep industry should be encouraged in every possible way, a country where every encouragement should be given to our farmers along that line. We should produce vast quantities of wool, and we should manufacture that wool into the finished article. I do not think it is possible for us to raise sheep as cheaply as they can be raised in Australia and New Zealand; consequently those countries can produce wool more cheaply than we can. But because of that fact are we to decide that we will go out of the sheep industry and let Australia and New Zealand supply our requirements? Hon. gentlemen like my hon. friend from Rosetown (Mr. Evans) take that position. It is the favourite attitude of the free-trader: let that country which is best adapted to the production of any particular article supply it to other countries not so well favoured, and let the latter devote themselves to some other line that they are best adapted to produce. I do not think that is a sound position to take, nor a position which any one of us in this Dominion dare take.
It has always appeared to me that the persons to be first considered in fixing a tariff schedule with respect to the woollen industry are our farmers who keep sheep and produce wool; and that to give them the encouragement which they deserve there should be a duty on wool to place them in a fair position in relation to their competitors in other countries enjoying certain climatic and other advantages. That in my judgment is where we should start in fixing a tariff on wool and wool products, our first object in view being the welfare of our farmers, the producers of wool; our second object should be the welfare of our manufacturers of woollen products, they being in a secondary position to the primary producers, the farmers.

My hon. friend who has just sat down (Mr. Evans) said that he has never heard a sound argument for protection. Of course, I cannot agree with him. I am not referring now to any arguments that I have attempted to advance in favour of protection; rather I have in mind tariff conditions in the various countries of the world. When I see their statesmen advocating protection, it seems to me that they at least are of average intelligence and capable of advancing sound arguments in favour of the protective principle. But let us take the country from which my hon. friend came; what about the Key Industries Act of the old country? What about the success which has followed the efforts of the British government in placing a comparatively high duty on the importation of automobiles? Even free-traders in England have come to the conclusion that certain industries are entitled to protection, and they are giving those industries protection. Under protection those industries are succeeding, with advantage to the working people of the old country, and with distinct advantage to the domestic consumers of the articles produced, because they are being produced under protection at a less cost than when those industries were operating under free trade. That is a situation which, I contend, strongly confirms the soundness of the protective principle.
But let me give another instance which comes right down to the question of tariff in relation to the woollen industry, the cotton industry, and so on. We have certain factories in the province of Ontario. Is it not a fact that we have in this provinoe of Ontario a minimum wage law, under which the owners of factories are obliged to pay a minimum rate of wages to their employees? They cannot go below a certain rate paid, for instance, to girls working in their factories. The law of the land compels the manufacturer to observe a certain standard, and the wages paid under this standard are found to be double the wages paid in some industries in England to girls employed in the same kind of work there. I venture to say that there is not a member of this house, not a member of the government, who would suggest for a moment that the minimum wage law should be abolished. That being so, we are at one on the necessity for a minimum standard of wages for our workmen. As I say, the minimum wage paid to the girls in these factories in Ontario is double the wage paid for similar work done by presumably just as efficient girls in England. Now, having subscribed to that law, of compelling the manufacturers to pay a certain wage, is it not logical to afford 
the manufacturers here some protection against foreign manufacturers producing the same kind of goods at a very much lower cost? The question may be argued from any point of view, but I argue from the standpoint of fair play. It is not because of what one government is doing; it is because the law of the land with respect to minimum wages places a certain responsibility upon the manufacturer in this country and leaves him at a decided disadvantage in competing with the manufacturers of similar goods in the old country where wages are lower.
The minimum wage law applies in Ontario ; does not the manufacturer in Ontario, according to my hon. friend's argument, deserve protection against low paid labour in Quebec?

The law is enforced in British Columbia too, I may say. My hon. friend's position as indicated by his question is not tenable. Within the bounds of a family there must be give and take; there is no getting away from that. You might as well say that the state of New York should impose no restrictions not acceptable to Pennsylvania, say. The fact is that the farmers of the northern states, New York, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Michigan are operating at a decided disadvantage in competition with the farmers in the southern states whose products are cheaper. But the northern farmers have no redress; there is no possible way of the difference being. overcome. In the northern states there is a severe winter to cope with, whereas climatic conditions in the south are advantageous. But it is a very different thing when you come to put on the statute books a law intended to protect the country from unfair competition from abroad, where the people do not help to pay our taxes. Obviously we cannot pass a law in Canada prohibiting the goods manufactured in Quebec, say, from entering Ontario, or the products of some other province being shipped to any other. Nevertheless the minimum wage law exists, and I submit that in all fairness, and logically, a country such as ours, with a minimum wage law enforced in certain provinces, should give some consideration to the manufacturers who are compelled to operate under that law. The minimum wage law places them in a position of disadvantage as compared with manufacturers producing similar goods in other countries where there is no such restriction.

My hon.
friend must know as well as I do that the object of the law is to ensure to the workers in industrial concerns in those provinces which have adopted it, a scale of wages which will make for a decent standard of living, a standard such as we think ought to obtain in Canada. We cannot dictate to England what its standard should be; it is for England to take action in that regard. But we can say, and we do say in Canada, in certain provinces at any rate, that girls working in our factories shall receive at least such a waqe as will afford them a fair chance in life; and we ought to say to England and to other countries as well, "We do not propose to let you send free into this country, to flood our markets, the products of cheap labour where the standard of living is below ours." My hon. friend from North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) spoke about England being a great customer of Canada and suggested that we should not impose restrictions upon her goods coming into this country, seeing that she freeiy admits most of our products.

I did not say that. What I did say was that if we did not take in return goods shipped from Great Britain, economic factors would compel her to go into the markets of the world where British goods are bought in return.

Great Britain will buy her wheat from the Argentine, the knifed States, India or from any other country if she can get it cheaper there than in Canada. British statesmen are not fools; they are not throwing away money; they will not pay 15 a bushel for Canadian wheat if they can get it at S4 a bushel from other countries.
Would it not be perfectly logical for us to buy our woollen goods where we could get them cheapest?

It would,
perhaps, from my' hon. friend's standpoint, if I can come to any conclusion as to what her politics amounts to. But we are laying down a policy for Canada and not for Great Britain, although it does seem to me that the government has been more concerned in fixing a fiscal policy in favour of the United States and other countries rather than for the benefit of the people of Canada. We are here to legislate for Canada, and I do not subscribe to the sentiments expressed by my hon. friend from North Winnipeg that because we are a part of the British Empire and because Great Britain buys freely from us, we should let down our tariff walls entirely, let our industries go to pot, and allow the

Surely there can be no question of that. W'hat has happened time after time? Consider the question of eggs.

I will admit that there is a good deal in the objection of the minister. I was making a general application of the argument, and I am quite sure the minister understood my point. I will not carry that further, because I do not want to take up the time of the com-

Way it and Means-Customs Tariff
mittee unnecessarily, although I believe if I wanted to argue the point of order I would have fairly good grounds upon which to do so. I got up to stress this point in regard to wool:	That inasmuch as we have in
this country a minimum wage law which has been endorsed by the members of this house -at least there has been no attempt made to get rid of it; I do not think any hon. member would advocate anything of the sort -that since we as a people, or as a government, or as a party, or as members of parliament have subscribed to that minimum wage law and thereby arbitrarily placed the manufacturers of woollens in this country at a disadvantage in competing with other countries that have not got a minimum wage law, in all fairness it is up to us to take that into consideration and give those manufacturers a reasonable amount of protection against cheaper production costs and unfair competition which has been forced on them. That is the position I take, and I was drawn into a discussion on other points. I do not wish to take up the minister's time unnecessarily but I was applying the argument in the case of woollens to the case of eggs, hay and other commodities, as the minister understood very well. However, I appreciate his desire to get along with business and I do not want to interfere unnecessarily or unfairly with that desire.
I will just say in conclusion that in the fixing of the schedules on woollens the position which I have always taken, no matter on which side of the house I sat, was that I believed that any government in this country approaching the matter from the right angle or the right viewpoint would consider it from the standpoint of the farmer, of the man who keeps the sheep and the man who produces the wool, and recognize that the manufacturer should be secondary to the producer.

This is
another item that looks to me very much like an increase, in spite of what the minister has said. He gave the importations under item 558, which was formerly dutiable, but he did not say anything about the imports under item 559, which was free. Has the minister the total value of the imports under item 559? This was free before; it is now dutiable. There is another item, 560, not included under this, which also was free. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I submit that there is nothing the matter with it. This is a concession to the trade, and as a result we shall have cheaper cloth.

This item affects an industry
in my own city, and I shall therefore endeavour to point out what is the matter with it. We discussed this question pretty fully last evening, particularly the hon. member
for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), whose city is also affected by this change in the tariff. The change, as I understand it, is this, that worsted yam, which previously had a reasonable protection of 12^ per cent against the British manufacturer, is now put on the free list. That leaves the manufacturer of worsted yarn without any protection at all against his English competitor. Under the protection that has been accorded this industry for several years, a good many of the factories engaged in woollen production have built up a business, and they manufacture the yarn for their own industry. It is not the raw material, as was pointed out by the Minister of Finance the other day; it is the material which is partly manufactured and represents about one-third of the labour in producing the finished commodity. In my city we have two industries engaged in woolen production, both under one management They have been manufacturing their own yarn. The persons employed in the manufacture of a portion of the production number 189, and the annual payroll is $141,704.
Now, I understand that the manufacturers have waited upon the Minister of Finance and presented their views. It is my purpose now to say a word or two on behalf of the men employed in the industry, for if these tariff changes become operative they are likely to lose their occupation, which to them would be a very serious matter. As we all know, the woollen industry has not been on a very good footing for some years, and many of the men engaged in these factories have had to be content with part time employment. The proposed changes will enable British manufacturers, emplojdng labour at a much lower scale of wages than obtains in Canada, to compete with our own manufacturers, and it is extremely likely that that portion of the mill in Peterborough in which the yarn ia produced will be forced to close down, thus throwing the men out of work. This condition will not be confined to Peterborough, it will exist in industries located in other towns which will be similarly affected, as was so ably pointed out last night by the hon. member for South Wellington. This being so, between seven and eight hundred men employed in the manufacture of Canadian yam are very likely to lose their employment. I would ask the minister to lay this matter over for another year, so that in the meantime the facts may be presented to him in a clearer fashion than is possible at the present time. What is gained by passing this item? What will be the resultant benefit to the consumer? Very few people are much in-
1652	COMMONS
Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
terested in whether they pay a few cents more or less for an article; but it is a very serious matter to those Canadian workmen who will have to face the prospect of unemployment. Again I ask the minister to let this subject stand for a year at any rate, in order that he may give it more careful consideration.

Mr. Chairman, I feel I cannot allow this item to pass without another word of protest. I should very much. like to find myself sharing the opinion of -the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) that this is an increase. But fine yams-40's and finer-came in under the old tariff at 12| per cent, and that is the only portion I am interested in. Practically all those yarns came from Great Britain. If there was any quid pro quo, so to speak, for the consuming public there might be some justification for this change in the tariff. The case has been so well presented by my hon. leader (Mr. Bennett), by my hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) and by my hon. friend from Peterborough (Mr. Peck) that I do not feel it necessary again to go over the ground that they have so ably covered. Let me take as an example of what would happen under this item to the selling price of an ordinary suit of clothes, valued at about $40. The actual cloth from the mill entering into that suit would be yards at about $2.25 per yard, or somewhere in the neighbourhood of $8. In other words, only 20 per cent of the cost of the suit is in the cloth. To manufacture that cloth-known as 14, 15 or 16 fine worsted, meaning 14 ounces, 15 ounces or 16 ounces to the yard-approximately a pound and an eighth or a pound and a quarter of yam yer yard is used. This shrinkage from a pound and a quarter of yam to a pound per yard of cloth is due to the fact that the natural oil of the wool and the lubricating oil that becomes impregnated in the yarn during the process of spinning are taken out in the scouring. If that 4J pounds of fine worsted yarn were purchased in the old country at to-day's price and at the current rate of exchange it would cost $1.28 per pound. The previous duty on worsted yarn^ was 12J per cent. According to my figuring, this would amount to 72 cents; the hon. member for South Wellington placed tlm duty at 60 cents. What would be the saving to the consumer, the man who buy3 the suit of clothes? If you could say to him "You will save anywhere from two to five dollars on a suit of clothes," then there would be some justification for this change in the tariff. But there is a saving of only 72 cents, and to effect this saving you are taking from 
the mills that spin their yarn to manufacture their woollen and worsted cloths practically 40 per cent of their business and putting it on a free trade basis. Up to the point where the wool is changed into fine yarn the work is done by the heads of families, the cleaning, scouring, carding and spinning involving heavy coarse labour. After the yam has gone through those processes it is put into the looms and handled by female help. So the damage that is being done to 40 per cent of the workers in these mills affects the heads of families, and consequently presents a very serious situation. To bring its gravity homo to the minister I need only cite two cases In one town of 3,500 people we have a mill employing a thousand hands, and in another town of about 5,000 people, a mill employing 228 hands. Those mills are typical of the industry. We have several of them in the constituency of South Waterloo. This part of the tariff schedule dealing with fine worsted yarns should be reconsidered, for the proposed change will give nobody any particular benefit, and it is fraught with serious consequences to many of our Canadian working people.

The light
has failed.

My hon.
friends to my left are always talking about the manufacturer being benefited by these tariff changes. Let me say that no manufacturer of yam is being benefited by this item; and there is no doubt that the 72 cents or the 60 cents, as the case may be, that is being saved under the tariff will not be passed on to the consumer. It will slightly reduce the cost of yarn, but it will put out of business a large part of the manufacturers' equipment. In the large mill I spoke of-it is located in Hespeler-the housing and spinning equipment represent an investment of practically one million dollars. In the other mill-located in Preston-the investment is between $400,000 and $500,000. I am not going to say that the employees in that mill will be thrown out of work entirely-

I cannot help saying a word or two in connection with this item, because it recalls to my mind that during the last election there were inserted in all the local papers in my constituency glaring advertisements to the effect that all people were divided into two classes: they were either Conservatives or Liberals. That conclusion was arrived at on the basis of their tariff policy. I have before me part of the old 1919 chart that has been referred to so often in this chamber? It is an old maxim that you have to keep repeating, repeating and repeating and after a while perhaps it will soak in. In this chart we have these words as to the doctrine of the Liberal party:

To my mind there is in this country a strong feeling and a demand that these schedules should be reduced, and if the electors in this country come to realize that they cannot accomplish a reduction along these lines through the Liberal party, which pledged itself to provide these reductions, the low tariff element in this country is going to find expression in some other way. It has done that before. In spite of the assistance that has been given to the government through the increase of low tariff sentiment on the government side of the house since the last election, by the acquisition of a larger number of low tariff men from the province of Ontario and from the western provinces, it seems to me that the government is proceeding in the opposite direction to lower tariffs, and that it is not reducing the tariff after all the preparations that have been made to effect a reduction. The tariff board has given a year's study to this subject, and the low tariff men are in larger numbers than ever before on the government benches, and yet we are asked to put through these schedules with the rates as high as I have mentioned.
The plea of the government used to be that they could accomplish something if they had stable government. But what is being accomplished in these schedules? The agricultural implement schedules were not nearly as high as these, and yet a substantial reduction was effected in them. The automobile duties and other tariffs corresponded with these now before us in rates of duty, and yet a substantial reduction was effected in them, but we have no reduction in these clothing schedules, in spite of the fact that we now have stable government, with the Liberals in a big majority in the house. The Minister of Finance last night, in giving his reasons why all these reductions were being made in the way of placing raw wool and cottons on the free list, said:
The tariff board in considering how they could best help the industry-
He is speaking of the woollen industry:
-had two ways open to them; they could either put up the duty on the finished product, or give a concession on the raw material required for the industry. They took the latter course, and I believe it is sound.

We asked for relief for the consumer, we asked for tariff reductions, and that is what we expected to get through our organization, the Consumers' League, but all we get is free raw materials for the manufacturers, and no corresponding reduction for the consumer. I feel that I should not let these tariff schedules pass without bringing them to the attention of the house to show the ridiculously high level at which they are being maintained. Let us remember that once these schedules are passed it is not at all likely that they will be referred to again for a number of years. speechtext: Yes, I sometimes have difficulty in hearing my hon. friend because-
Because of the continual chatter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -because ,of the busy atmosphere around me. I have told the house at least three times that in the budget we were serving notice on the world that in October we intended changing the percentage of British workmanship to qualify imports under the British preference. Australia had represented to us that 75 per cent would be fair; I think New Zealand suggested 75 per cent also; I do not recall whether South Africa favoured 50 or 75 per cent. We always took the position that 50 per cent would be about fair. Indeed, looking at our own exports to other countries, we were not very much interested in having the percentage higher than 50. This will be done, as it has been done before, by regulations issued by the governor in council. But we are not going to disqualify our own importers in any way by making the percentage of British labour content so high that the goods cannot come in. We want them. But we do not want the middleman on the docks at Liverpool to bring in goods fiom continental countries and then ship them here under the British preference, thus preventing British workmen from getting any part of the advantage of this change. We are not going beyond what the British manufacturers themselves have imposed upon our industries. gentleman will read the table printed at the end of the Prime Minister's speech the other day he will find some differences there.

Yes, on the basis of
speeches, but I am speaking of the schedules.
I was speaking of the actual record.

But what about these
items? Here are increases of 10 per cent in the British preference, and 5 and 7 per cent in the intermediate and general rates. What difference is there in this instance?

I would point out to the
hon. gentleman that in item 574a there is a reduction from 25 to 20 per cent in the British preference. In item 574b there is an increase of 5 per cent.

Nothing comes from
Great Britain under that item. The imports all come in from the United States.

I will give you the imports from Great Britain and the United States under item 574b, in 1026: United States, $144,801; United Kingdom, $47,649. There is actually a decrease in this item from 25 to 20 per cent.

I do not know what my
hon. friend is quoting from, but I have the record here. I will admit that it is compiled by this government, and it may be faulty, but I cannot be charged with that. For the year 1926 I find that "webbing, elastic, over one inch in width," was imported from the United Kingdom to the amount of $15,900, and from the United States, $389,000; other countries, $267.
The hon. gentleman is referring to 574b?

It is not described as
574a or 574b in the trade returns. It is described as "webbing, elastic, over one inch in width," and in the item before us it is described as "webbing with strands of rubber," which is elastic, "interwoven or braided therein, exceeding one inch but not exceeding twelve inches in width."

The items are changed. I
admit that the imports were $389,199 from the United States, and $15,992 from England. This item is changed to 574b, but the other item, 574a, refers to narrow goods, and under that item there was imported from the United States goods to the amount of $144,800, and from the United Kingdom, $47,649.

What does the addition

speechtext: It is asked for by the National Revenue department to make it plain that belting for machinery is covered, not other kinds-for instance, body belts.
There are conveyer belts.

speechtext: They would be classified as machinery.
I suppose this includes threshing machine belts?

Is this the rate that will be paid by manufacturers for belting in their own factories?

Is this also the rate that will be paid for repairs for agricultural machinery?

speechtext: No, I should think it would be whatever the agricultural machinery rate is.
I know that when a threshing machine is sold the drive belt is priced separately; it does not go with the machine. Is this the rate that will be paid for repairs for agricultural machinery?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, it will come in under
whatever the classification for the machinery may be. Threshing machines come under 447b: Wind-stackers, and threshing machine separators, including baggers, weighers, and self-feeders therefor, and complete parts thereof, 5 per cent, 10 per cent, 10 per cent. That would be the classification.
Does the connecting or drive belt go at the same rate as the rest of the machine?

speechtext:
I am advised that it would
come as a complete part of the machine, but I am inclined to agree that if a hardware merchant in a country village handled material of this kind bought in rolls it would come under one of these classifications; it would not be a complete part.
Mr. FANiSHER (Lambton): How is it that this belting comes under the same classification as silk and artificial silk?

speechtext:

610.

speechtext:
Resolved, that schedule B to the customs tariff, being chapter 44 of the revised statutes of Canada, 1027, be amended by striking thereout tariff items 1011, 1012, 1024, 1029, the enumeration of goods, and the rates of drawback of customs duties set opposite to each of the said items, and the following items, enumerations and rates of drawback of customs duties be inserted in the said schedule
B.	. ,
Customs tariff-1011. Botany yarn, single, numbers thirty and finer, on mule cops, tubes or cones, or in hanks, dry spun on the French or Belgian systems, in white only, not doubled or twisted, subject to drawback when used prior to the first day of October, 1928, in the manufacture of socks and stockings and jersey cloth-payable as drawback 99 per cent.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is there any change?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The only change is that this
drawback expires on September 30, 1928.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There was no date before. Why is the drawback entirely removed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The drawback was given to establish this industry, under the French and Belgian systems. It is well established now and it is considered reasonable that they should pay their share. It comes under a 10 per cent item.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: In other words, they are going to be protected under the tariff and the drawback is taken away?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Customs tariff-1012. Woven fabrics in the web, subject to drawback when used in the manufacture of linings for hats and caps, or in the manufacture of hat shapes, and bonnet shapes, made from buckram-payable as drawback 99 per cent.
[Mr. Spemer.l

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Buckram was covered by a special item in the tariff and was free for purposes of bookbinding.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is for hats.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There is a drawback of 99 per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

According to
my information, under the old tariff a drawback of 99 per cent was allowed on a completed lining. That item has been withdrawn, and it now reads; "Woven, fabrics in the web when used in the manufacture of lining for hats and caps" as amended. There is no objection to the item as it stands, as is pointed out in a letter which I have received. The writer says:
Paragraph 1012 under the old tariff allowed a drawback of 99 per cent on completed linings. This item has been withdrawn and it now reads, "Woven fabrics in the web when used in the manufacture of linings for hats and caps."' While this will be satisfactory providing we will he permitted to engage the help from the United States necessary to print and make up the linings, we call your attention to the fact that we have now at least 1,800 dozens of linings in stock on which we paid a duty of 37J per cent expecting a drawback of 99 per cent on same after we put these into hats and shipped them to consumers. We sold these linings practically at cost and depended on the drawback to avoid a loss. For instance, a lining for which we charged $3 per dozen cost us $2.93 per dozen after being put in the hat. You can see by this that we had to figure on the drawback to avoid a loss.
If this item cannot or will not be changed then we would like to 1m permitted either to receive the drawback until June 1, when our spring season ends and our fall season commences. or not have these tariff items enforced until then.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am disposed to meet my
hon. friend on that, but I do not see just how that can be done.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
As it stands now there
is a drawback of 99 per cent in perpetuity, or until amended. Is that not so?

speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Then there is no question of the drawback whether the material is used to-day, to-morrow or any time.

There is a
different wording in the present drawback.

speechtext: Let me see if I understand my hon. friend correctly. The industry in bis constituency has imported the linings and manufactured them. That is now changed.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It must be imported in.
the web, and that was not the case formerly.
