speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am afraid I will be unable
to help my hon. friend. I think he had better take his chances, together with everyone else.
If these imports were made before this change took place, would it not be a matter of justice that these drawbacks should be allowed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
All these changes became
effective on February 17. My hon. friend's industry is in no worse position than any other industry in Canada. I have given him a considerable concession to-night, and I hope he will not press this point because it would be establishing a precedent which might become very expensive.

Would not the minister
consider that any importation made prior to the passing of the budget would be entitled to the drawback when claimed, although it might not be claimed before the passing of the budget? I think that might be done in the administration of these items.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a matter for consideration by the Department of National Revenue, and it might be passed upon by the treasury board, although I am not sure of that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: If the minister will observe, item 1011 fixes the date of October 1, 1929, within which certain named articles are to be used; item 1024 is in almost similar terms, but item 1012 places no limitation upon the time within which the rebate or drawback is to operate. As I understand the contention submitted to the committee it is that you should apply the same principle with respect to the intermediate item as to the other two. I think this is only precautionary, because I fancy the officers of the department will say, "Where the goods have been actually imported and the duty paid, the rate of rebate would apply as it then was", but apparently the government thought it advisable in the other two items to which I have referred to fix a date, namely October 1, 1929. Is it quite right that you should do that in those cases while leaving the intermediate item in such a condition that it will create a hardship amounting to financial loss with regard to the parties interested?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: These parties waited on me, and I do not think this will amount to very much. Of course this gentleman wants every dollar he can get, for which I do not blame him, but we made concessions to him to-night on four different items. I think he had better take his chances in connection with this item along with the other people.

I would like to call the attention of the minister to section 10 of the Customs Tariff Act regarding drawbacks, which is as follows:
On the materials set forth in schedule B to this act, when used for consumption in Canada, for the purpose specified in that schedule, there may be paid, out of the consolidated revenue fund, the several rates of drawback of customs duties set opposite to each item respectively in that schedule, under regulations by the governor in council.
So the governor in council has it within his power to pay that drawback under that section.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will make no commitment to-night, but if my colleague should recommend that and next year it is found that we have consented to it, I hope my hon. friend will not deal too harshly with us.
We will hold him immune for anything of this kind.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman does not want to be unduly hasty.

speechtext: I am on my feet at the present time and it would be well for the hon. gentleman to observe that fact. I had representations made to me by the paper manufacturers. They stated that the resolution as introduced would be pretty wide. For instance it was represented
fMr Bennett.]
to me that it would enable large mail order houses sending out their advertising matter to get paper under the regulations as they were originally presented and receive the drawback. item apply now?

speechtext: About how much money will be involved?

speechtext:

Item as amended agreed to.

speechtext:
I beg to move that the following be substituted for drawback item 1061:
1061. Woven fabric manuactured for covering the outside of books, of a class or kind not made in Canada. When used by bookbinders in binding books in their own factories-99 per cent.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: This item certainly is somewhat in conflict with the buckram item to which reference was made the other evening. Buckram is the word which was used in the linen schedule. speechtext: I may be mistaken but I was under the impression there was an item dealing with buckram for bookbinding.

speechtext:

Cloth such as is used for covering the outside of books when imported for use exclusively in binding books, under regulations by the Minister of Customs:	British preferential
tariff, free; intermediate tariff, free; general tariff, free.
In this case we changed the tariff item into a drawback item because we learned the tariff item was being abused.

I am, perhaps, a little dense, but item 531, which is still in the tariff, deals with cloth used for covering the outside of books. That is free. The item we are dealing with here is woven fabric manufactured for covering the outside of books and is subject to a drawback of 99 per cent. How can you get a drawback of 99 per cent on an article that is free of duty?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The free item has been
repealed.

The minister said a
moment ago it is still in the tariff.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It may come in under the item of coloured linens or cottons, but the drawback of 99 per cent is paid when the fabric is used for covering books.
Can the minister give us the new item w-hich takes the place of 531?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Whatever classification it comes into now the bookbinders will get back 99 per cent of the duty if the material is used for bookbinding purposes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
That is a new item in the
tariff.
Formerly it was free. Now there is a drawback of 99 per cent.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: And there is a duty on it.
Somewhere, but we do not know wheTe it is.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friends will surely admit that there may be a difference in classification.
What I am trying to find out is where it is. We have repealed the old item, we cannot find the new item, and we are providing for a drawback of 99 peT cent. That is the position we are in.

speechtext: My hon. friend will understand that any fabric, no matter what it is, imported for covering the outside of books will get a 99 per cent drawback.

item 540 in the new tariff.

speechtext:
I am interested now only in the preparation of the tariff itself and not in the question of duty or no duty. Tariff item 569b reads:
Hat sweats, cap peaks, hatters' tips-
And so on. This is now free under all tariffs. I turn to the drawback item and I find these words:
When imported by manufacturers of hat sweats, hat peaks and hatters' tips-
And so on. These are the same words exactly and there is a drawback of 99 per cent. How can there be a drawback of 99 per cent on a free item?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It might not be the same
item.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The words in the tariff
item are exactly the same as in the drawback item. Under the tariff item the rates are free, free, free, and now there is going to be 99 per cent drawback.

speechtext:
They are going into another
classification.

speechtext: There cannot be another classification when the words are the same. Is there a nigger in the woodpile? If there is, let us smoke him out.

speechtext:

originally prepared item 569b was dutiable at 5 per cent on the intermediate and 7i per cent on the general tariff.

speechtext: When the tariff came into the house the other day item 569b was not free under all tariffs, but now it is free under all tariffs, the 5 per cent and the 7i per cent having been struck out.

items.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I beg to move that the following be substituted for drawback item 1065:
Customs tariff

1065. Bituminous coal, when used in melting, evaporating and preparing salt produced in Canada: Provided that no drawback under this item shall be payable on coal used in producing salt or brine when such salt or brine is further manufactured than salt enumerated in tariff items 40, 41, 42, and 42a-payable as drawback, 99 per cent.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Would the minister tel!
us approximately what sums are paid by way of drawback at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I could not but I will get
an estimate of that for my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The whole sum of money paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will try to get that for
my hon. friend on Monday.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Our drawbacks are increasing very steadily. According to the last annual report we paid some $15,000,000 odd in drawbacks.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That possibly would include
goods that had been exported to other countries. Does my hon. friend want that separated?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The minister is asking
the very question to which I desired to direct the attention of the committee. Originally drawbacks were a form of legislation used for the purpose of encouraging export trade. Whenever we imported raw materials of any kind and manufactured in Canada a product from them, on the goods that went out of the country we gave a drawback to the manufacturer. This of course was a great encouragement to the manufacturing business of the country. It stimulated foreign trade

Ways and Means-Drawbacks
and provided a ready means by which we kept our factories engaged in export business. That principle has been departed from. This principle proposes to grant a drawback for domestic manufactures for use in our own country. This means that you subsidize each individual man who comes within it to the extent to which he may use the particular material that is subject to the drawback. In this instance it happens to be coal. There are, we will say for the sake of argument, 100,000 tons of coal used by a particular person. There is, we will say for the sake of argument, a duty of ten cents a ton involved in it; that is $10,000. He gets a present of $10,000 because he happens to be engaged in a particular industry or a particular business. His neighbour, engaged in another line of business, in which he is consuming the same material, gets no such assistance from the treasury. Now I put it to the minister that the principle involved is wrong. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has explained why he has done it. He has an industry in his community that was affected by it. It has cost $60,000 to dredge the river to enable the ships to get up and bring the coal in, because one ship got stuck there. That is what happened; you will find it in the estimates. It has cost this country $60,000 or more to get the wharf and facilities to unload the coal that is to go to this particular industry. After the coal has been used in that industry, although there may be an industry across the street using the same kind of material for steam, there will be no drawback. At the end of the season one gets $10,000 in cash from the government because he sells his product in Canada, and the other gets nothing. That is discrimination of the worst character. That is not a proper performance, I submit, of the duties of government. I should like to know, if possible, just what we are paying out in drawbacks now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will try and get the figures for my hon. friend.

In considering
drawbacks, has the minister considered the advisability of allowing a similar drawback in respect of coal used in the production of rolled iron and steel, pulverized?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have a resolution to present as soon as this item is carried. I am not sure that it covers the product to which my hon. friend refers.

Was
this item considered by the tariff board?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What was considered by the tariff board was an application by the salt manufacturers of Canada. They made an application, which was considered by the board, and with respect to which some evidence was given. The salt producers did not ask for this sort of protection at all. They pointed out certain conditions that existed, and they desired that legislation should be introduced that would place them on an equality with other producers of salt. The Minister of Trade and Commerce says that this is the way he has selected to do it. In other words, he has selected to give a present to particular people engaged in a particular business, as against their neighbours, rather than to make it of general application in which all might share. The principle is wrong. In this case it is barefaced favouritism, that is all, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce has himself admitted it.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
Item as amended agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I beg to move, Mr. Chairman, that the following drawback item, enumerations and rates of drawbacks of duty be inserted in schedule B to the customs tariff:
Customs tariff-1066. Bituminous coal when pulverized by proprietors of rolling mills for heating iron or steel for use only in the production of rolled iron or steel at their rolling mills-payable as drawback 99 per cent.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Item agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I beg to move to substitute the following for tariff item 219a:
Customs tariff-219a. Non-alcoholic preparations or chemicals for disinfecting, dipping or spraying, n.o.p.; materials, n.o.p., for use only in producing or manufacturing preparations specified in this item, under regulations prescribed by the Minister of National Revenue: British preferential tariff, free; intermediate tariff free; general tariff, free.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
Item as amended agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
With respect to 219b, I beg to move that the following item, enumerations and rates of duty be inserted in schedule A:
Customs tariff-219b. Formaldehyde, containing not more than 15 per centum of alcohol: British preferential tariff, free; intermediate tariff, free; general tariff, free.
It has been represented to me that this is used largely for treating grain to prevent smut and I am now moving that formaldehyde be made free under all tariffs.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
To be consistent, the
government must place this item on the free list, but the effect of it upon one of the industries of this country the only one, as the

Ways and Means-Drawbacks

minister is aware, is going to be disastrous. Assuming two bushels of seed wheat to the acre, the protection afforded by this item is fifty-nine thousandths of a cent per 'bushel. It simply means the existence or the nonexistence of the industry in Canada. Is it desirable that we should have to import this very necessary material for the prevention of smut on wheat, or that we should be willing to pay fifty-nine thousandths of a cent per bushel protection? That is the question.
Whom does the hon. gentleman mean by "we"?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I mean parliament.
It is the farmer who will pay it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Yes. He will pay fifty-nine thousandths of a cent per bushel, and I ask, is it desirable that he should find himself in the position where none of this material will be manufactured in Canada, or that he should possibly have to pay fifty-nine thousandths of a cent per bushel and have his source of supply in Canada? Representations were made to me, and I assume to other hon. members, and the books were open to the minister, and the facts submitted to him. I have no interest in the matter beyond that of a citizen to whom these papers were sent, as they were no doubt to large numbers of the members of this house. I am certain that the minister is satisfied that it involves only fifty-nine thousandths of a cent per bushel.
Does not the hon. gentleman admit that putting on that amount of duty would increase the price of the article to the consumer?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Assuming that it does,
it means only fifty-nine thousandths of a cent per bushel, and I ask, is it desirable that the Canadian farmer dhould be dependent upon an imported supply of this very necessary material, or that he should possibly pay fifty-nine thcfhsandths of a cent per bushel to have this supply in Canada?
It is a small matter to argue about.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Yes, but it means the
life or death of an industry in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A representative of that industry complained to me that it would put him out of business, and eventually the farmers of Canada would pay more for the article. My answer to him was that the farmers wanted this, and I supposed they knew their business. That is why I brought in the resolution.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is it quite fair?

A step in the right
direction.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Is it a step in the right
direction to render it impossible for this industry to function here?-an industry that has reduced its capital stock from 86,000,000 to 82,000,000, whose books have been open to the minister and the officers of the department, whose officials I never saw until the dajr they interviewed the minister, and who left with the member for Rosetown the same document they left with me. I ask hon. members representing rural sections whether or not it is desirable to place the production of this very necessary article wholly in the hands of people outside of Canada who may be able to make the price anything they desire, and who will do so. We have had experience of it. There is no reason why we should not mention the industry. It is the Standard Chemical Company, owned in Great Britain. As I say, they had to reduce their capital from six to two million, because of their unsuccessful endeavour to establish a great industry in Canada. And any hon. gentleman who represents a rural riding knows how very powerful this particular disinfectant is. The hon. member for Saskatoon perhaps will be able to correct my description. It is a most powerful germicide, and, I understand, is used very largely in the fumigation of ships and buildings wherein people have been subject to infectious diseases. A very weak solution is used to prevent, so far as possible, a smut in wheat. Formaldehyde is composed of oxygen, nitrogen and carbon, so combined chemically as to form a very powerful germicide.
Now, if the possible effect of the tariff upon the price to the farmer is the very insignificant sum I have mentioned, are we wise in departing from that very limited protection, and thus placing our market entirely in the hands of mass-producing competitors? The important thing to remember is that this substance is produced in very large quantities in other countries where there is a great demand for it, whereas in Canada, owing to a limited market, it is produced in very small quantities. I can only reiterate that when the other day my attention was directed to this matter for the first time, I checked up the figures with some degree of care, and I said then I believe-and I still believe-that if the representatives of the rural constituencies were satisfied that only the insignificant amount mentioned was involved, they would not desire to destroy the industry in this country and place our farm population at the

St. Lawrence River Bridge Company
mercy of the chemical trust to the south of us. That is the problem for hon. members , to consider, and I am quite content with their judgment upon it.
My business for the moment in the position I occupy is to direct the attention of the committee to the fact and ask the minister if my statement of those facts is not correct, because, I submit, it is not sound for any minister of finance merely to say that it has been represented to him by the farm population that they wanted a certain thing, when, as he must now admit, they were not given the facts on which to base a correct conclusion. In my experience extending over thirty-six years I have observed no unfairness in the attitude of my fellow-Canadians when they have been fully seized of the facts. The minister told the people interested that they had made out a case, that the protection wa3 insignificant and in his judgment very reasonable. Now, because pressure has been brought to bear by others without the facts being placed before them, he says: I will remove the item from the tariff and put it on the same basis as the others, regardless of the effect of my action on the industry. I submit that that is not fair to the representatives of the rural constituencies who have not had an opportunity to be advised of the facts. I think it is the duty of the minister to place the facts before the house, not simply to say: Because somebody said they wanted me to do thus and so, I have done it. That is the position we must take in a matter of this kind.
Carried.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I do not propose that
this item shall pass to-night. We may as well make up our minds to it now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is eleven o'clock. All I
have to observe is that when I first brought these resolutions to the attention of the house, my hon. friend rather censured me because I was putting a tariff on formaldehyde

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I did not do that.
Progress reported.

speechtext:
